activities.anchor: European overseas empire ran in three distinct modes
activities.caption: line up the three waves, earliest first
activities.name: ceWavesOrder

config.prompt: Conquest, companies, scramble — order the waves, earliest first:
items: conquest and settlement: Cortés tops the Aztec state (1519–21), Pizarro the Inca (1532–33)
company empires: the British East India Company conquers Bengal after Plassey — 1757
the Berlin Conference sets the scramble's rules — 1884–85
within about two decades, roughly 90% of Africa is under European claim
config.why: The modes differed — settler, corporate, administrative — but the direction never did: power, capital and decisions flowed to Europe.

activities.anchor: The syllabus's first question deserves its own ledger
activities.caption: file each motive in its column
activities.name: ceMotivesBuckets

items.label: raw materials, captive markets and profitable outlets for capital — Hobson (1902), Lenin (1916)
the trading-company accounts, unambiguous about motive
coaling stations, naval bases, the Suez lifeline to India
'defence of India' rationalising a chain of acquisitions from Egypt to Somaliland — the 'official mind'
Fashoda (1898) — Britain and France nearly at war over a derelict fort
Kipling's 'white man's burden' (1899) and France's mission civilisatrice

config.why: Economic and strategic interests drove decisions; the civilising claim licensed them at home — and the gap between the claim and the ledgers is where the critical reading of empire lives.

activities.caption: pair each passenger of the exchange with its effect
activities.name: ceExchangeMatch

config.prompt: Two biospheres fused — pair each passenger with its effect:

pairs.right: went east, feeding the population booms that helped power Europe's and China's growth
killed an estimated 50–90% of Indigenous Americans within roughly a century of contact
drove both the enslavement of Africans and the importation of indentured workers

config.why: The largest demographic collapse in recorded history, often moving ahead of the Europeans themselves — conquest was cheap largely because disease had already collected.

activities.anchor: The trade was a triangle of coercion
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the forced migration
activities.name: ceTradeEstimate

config.prompt: Between 1501 and 1866, roughly how many Africans were shipped to the Americas?
config.why: An estimated 12.5 million (the Slave Voyages database's running census); perhaps 1.8 million died in the Middle Passage, and mortality began at the inland marches before any ship.
config.context: Brazil received about five million; North America, notably, received under half a million — yet grew to four million enslaved by 1860.

activities.anchor: The impacts that followed were a family, not a norm
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the scramble's varieties
activities.name: ceScrambleSpot

config.prompt: One line of this scramble briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: The Berlin Conference required 'effective occupation' and mutual recognition among the powers — with no African representative.
Leopold's Congo Free State was a private estate whose rubber quota regime killed, by careful modern estimates, millions.
The Herero and Nama genocide (1904–08) marked the century's first genocide.
Ethiopia was partitioned at Berlin and lost its independence.
Indirect rule governed cheaply through appointed chiefs, freezing 'traditional' authority into administrative furniture.
config.correction: Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa (1896) and stayed independent; Liberia, founded by freed American slaves, kept nominal sovereignty.
config.why: The varied impact is the point: empire's experience depended on what you were standing on and what was under your feet.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — after 1857, the restructured Raj
activities.name: ceRajCloze

config.text: The East India Company was abolished and the Crown took direct rule — the %%0%% (1858); the army was reorganised around distrust; policy turned to %%1%%; the Indian National Congress began as an elite petitioning forum in %%2%%; and the partition of Bengal (%%3%%) triggered the mass Swadeshi movement.
config.hint: The rising's real importance lies in what the British did afterwards — resistance shaped the empire's institutions as much as empire shaped its subjects.

activities.caption: drag the divider — claim versus practice
activities.name: ceClaimCompare

config.prompt: The empire that denied being one — drag the divider:

before.label: the claim
before.text: Liberation language: Washington speaks of freeing Cuba and the Philippines, and the anti-imperial Constitution is tested against imperial practice.

after.label: the practice
after.text: Cuba's Platt Amendment (1901) — intervention rights and the Guantánamo lease, still held; Puerto Rico a territory, and remains one; the Philippine-American War (1899–1902) kills thousands of Americans and hundreds of thousands of Filipinos.

config.why: The syllabus's cleanest study of motive versus claim — and Mark Twain's Anti-Imperialist League said the era's honest sentence about it.

activities.anchor: How the story is told is itself a colonial artifact
activities.caption: true or false — reading empire's ledger
activities.name: ceSaidJudge

statements.s: Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) showed how the scholarship itself constructed 'the East' as Europe's manageable other.
statements.why: The subaltern studies school then mined colonial archives against their grain to recover voiceless perspectives.

statements.s: The Belgian Congo had fewer than 20 university graduates among roughly 13 million people at independence (1960).
statements.why: The infrastructure served extraction, and education was deliberately capped.

statements.s: Empire's roads and railways were built mainly to develop the colonies for their own peoples.
statements.why: The audit says the infrastructure served extraction — read the administrators' documents as advocacy, not transcript.

statements.s: Empires met resistance from the start, not just at the end.
statements.why: Túpac Amaru II (1780), the Haitian Revolution, the Ashanti wars, Maji Maji (1905–07), Amritsar (1919) — resistance was constant, not epilogue.
